lesson.title: The Power Rule, Run in Reverse
lesson.summary: The power rule for integration states that ∫x^n dx = x^(n+1)/(n+1) + C for any exponent n except -1, obtained by undoing the differentiation power rule.
lesson.body:
You already know the power rule for derivatives: d/dx[x^n] = n x^(n-1), which brings the exponent down as a multiplier and lowers the exponent by one. Since integration is the reverse of differentiation, it makes sense that there should be a power rule for integration too, and it should undo exactly what the derivative version does.

That rule is: ∫x^n dx = x^(n+1)/(n+1) + C, valid for any exponent n except n = -1. In words: raise the exponent by one, then divide by that new exponent, then add the constant of integration. Notice how this is the mirror image of the derivative power rule. Differentiating lowers the exponent and multiplies by the old exponent; integrating raises the exponent and divides by the new exponent. If you differentiate the right-hand side, you should recover x^n exactly, and that is precisely how this rule was discovered: by asking what expression differentiates back to x^n.

Let's verify this with a full worked example. Take ∫x^5 dx. Here n = 5, so n + 1 = 6, and the rule gives x^6/6 + C. Check by differentiating: d/dx[x^6/6] = (1/6) · 6x^5 = x^5, which matches the integrand exactly.

The rule also works for negative exponents, as long as n is not exactly -1. Take ∫x^(-3) dx. Here n = -3, so n + 1 = -2, and the rule gives x^(-2)/(-2) + C, which can be written as -1/(2x^2) + C. Check by differentiating: d/dx[-(1/2)x^(-2)] = -(1/2) · (-2)x^(-3) = x^(-3), which again matches the integrand.

The one exponent excluded from this rule is n = -1. If you tried to apply the formula to ∫x^(-1) dx, you would need to divide by n + 1 = 0, which is undefined. The antiderivative of x^(-1) = 1/x does exist, but it is not a power function at all; it involves the natural logarithm, and it is handled by a separate rule covered later. For every other exponent, though, positive, negative, or a fraction, this single formula does the job.
